paragraphs: R' Yudan, father of R' Mattanya.

He is mentioned in the Yerushalmi: Demai chapter 5, halakhah 3, and chapter 7, halakhah 4; Sheviit, beginning of chapter 10; Orlah chapter 1, halakhah 3; Challah chapter 4, halakhah 2; Shabbat chapter 1, halakhah 9, and chapter 9, halakhah 1; Eruvin chapter 2, halakhah 4; Chagigah chapter 2, halakhah 5; Moed Katan chapter 1, halakhah 7; Nazir chapter 5, halakhah 1; Avodah Zarah chapter 1, halakhah 1, and chapter 3, halakhot 3 and 5. In Kilayim chapter 3, end of halakhah 1, [he appears as] ‘R' Yudan avuha de-R' Matlia’; in Taanit chapter 1, halakhah 3, ‘R-Y avoi de-R' Matna’; in Yevamot chapter 1, at the supplied locator דה״א, ‘R-Y abba de-R' Matnita’; and in Ketubot, beginning of chapter 4, ‘R-Y avoi de-R' Yudah avoi de-R' Mattanyah.’ Hyman says all of them should read ‘R' Yudan avoi de-R' Mattanya.’ He continues: ‘And as we explained in the entry R' Mattanyah, who was in the fourth and fifth generations of the Amoraim of Eretz Israel, then his father was without doubt at the beginning of the fourth generation.’

notes.text: The text gives Matlya, Matna, Matnita and an additional father chain before proposing Mattanya throughout. The printed Yevamot locator דה״א is irregular.

All personal titles are abbreviated in Hyman’s supplied text and remain R-prime here. His three R-Y forms are retained as initials, contextually pointing back to Yudan; a full Rabbi in another passage is not transferred into them. The five whole saved Guggenheimer scalars show אבוי דרבי מתנית in the second halakhah of Yevamot chapter 1; the supplied דה״א remains unresolved, without guessing a damaged numeral. Ketubot 4:1 retains the additional Yudan–Yudah–Mattanyah father chain, with full Rabbi titles in that named digital passage; Kilayim 3:1 has אבויי דרבי מתניא, Taanit 1:3 has מתניה and Sheviit 10:1 has מתנייה. These edition-specific forms do not replace Hyman’s Matlia, Matna or Matnita, remove the additional generation, or prove how a different reading arose. The heading and proposed correction have מתניא, while Ketubot and the final cross-reference have מתניה; both forms are preserved. Avoi, avuha and abba remain the distinct supplied father-formula spellings. Beginning of Sheviit chapter 10 and Ketubot chapter 4 is retained; the older end-of-chapter and inferred Yevamot-halakhah-1 readings remain historical only. Hyman’s all-should-read instruction is his definite proposed harmonization; his we-explained first-person plural, fourth-and-fifth-generation placement and without-doubt beginning-of-the-fourth-generation conclusion retain their force as his chronological inference. No father chain or chronology is admitted as an identity fact. The other listed loci were not newly checked; the surrounding legal material in the selected primary scalars is not added to this notice. All historical English, notes and the source hold remain unchanged.

The consulted scan of Hyman, volume II, printed p. 617, contains the notice across the two columns, retaining the different patronymic forms, the extra Yudah in the Ketubot chain, and his instruction to read Mattanya throughout. The five whole consulted Guggenheimer passages support the local comparisons already recorded: Yevamot’s named paragraph is in chapter 1, halakhah 2; Ketubot 4:1 retains the additional father; and Kilayim 3:1, Taanit 1:3 and Sheviit 10:1 give their own Mattanya forms. These observations do not authorize deletion of a generation or harmonization of distinct names. The supplied irregular Yevamot locator is not silently repaired. The other listed loci and the exact historical editions have not all been collated here. Hyman’s all-should-read instruction and his without-doubt chronological conclusion remain his explicit arguments, rather than independently established genealogy or dates.
